issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of toxic chemical exposure. 'Specific body parts associated with the event,' 'power imbalance,' and 'being alone with women' are much more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual assault formulations than toxic exposure.

issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items point to incompatible trauma meanings: body-part cues, gendered interpersonal cues, and power-over-me situations imply an assaultive perpetrator context rather than an occupational chemical exposure event.

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male bomb disposal technician whose index trauma is toxic chemical exposure, 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-related trigger. It implies an interpersonal/sexual-threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the threat items, which instead reflect generalized physical danger/hypervigilance.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure, which typically does not involve an identifiable perpetrator. This item suggests an assault/interpersonal trauma formulation and is inconsistent with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: Avoiding new relationships is hard to reconcile with a 62-year-old married bomb disposal technician whose indexed trauma is toxic chemical exposure; this strategy fits interpersonal trauma or betrayal formulations more than exposure-related PTSD, and there are no corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal items to support an interpersonal-relationship focus.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone in a room or building does not connect well to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe generalized hypervigilance and escape planning, while the trauma type and other selected triggers do not suggest solitary settings as a specific danger cue. This looks like a maladaptive strategy for a symptom pattern not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is difficult to integrate with toxic chemical exposure and the rest of the selected profile. The other triggers are workplace and loud noises, and the threat items reflect environmental danger monitoring rather than coercion or dominance. This trigger suggests an interpersonal/control-based trauma theme that is unsupported elsewhere.

vignette:
Kwame was fifty-eight when the call came in about a suspicious package in a downtown parking garage. After thirty-four years as a bomb disposal technician, he had learned to read the subtle signs—the geometry of a circuit, the faint smell of homemade accelerant—but nothing had prepared him for the tear-gas canister rigged to release a chemical agent. In the moment of detonation, there was a deafening crack that seemed to split the air itself, and then a fine, burning mist enveloped him. He felt his throat seize, his eyes stream, and when he finally crawled out of the garage, his hands shaking, an ambulance was already waiting. The antiseptic sting of alcohol wipes and the sharp, clean smell of the hospital corridor would become the scent of his worst memory.

For the first few weeks after the exposure, Kwame told himself he was fine. He returned to work as soon as the doctors cleared him, saying nothing about the way his heart hammered when a colleague slammed a locker door. He began to notice that he could not sit still in the break room; his eyes would drift from the door to the windows to the ceiling vents, cataloging every possible way out before he could even think about coffee. It became automatic, almost a second job: scanning the room for danger the moment he entered any indoor space. At home, his wife Miriam would place a hand on his shoulder to get his attention, and he would flinch so hard he nearly knocked over a table. He started sleeping with the bedroom door open, even though he had always liked the privacy, because being alone in a closed room felt like being trapped in the garage again.

The triggers multiplied quietly. A sudden bang from a car backfiring on his street would send him into a cold sweat, his mind replaying the crack of the canister. A routine physical at the clinic, with its bleached sheets and the faint chemical scent of disinfectant, made him feel so lightheaded that he left before the doctor could even take his blood pressure. He began avoiding hospitals altogether, and when Miriam asked him to come for her own appointment, he made an excuse about overtime. That was true, in a way: Kwame had started working twelve-hour shifts, then fourteen, then sixteen. He told himself he was dedicated, that the unit needed his experience, but what he could not say aloud was that when he was focused on a dismantled fuse or a schematic, he could not hear the echoes of the garage in his head. Work became a container, a place where he could be safe because he was never alone with his thoughts. Over the months, the overtime became a habit, and Miriam began sleeping alone more often than not.

What frightened Kwame most was the sense that danger was still there, even when he knew it was not. He would stand at the entrance to a supermarket and identify three exit routes before stepping inside. In a restaurant, he sat facing the door and made sure he could see the kitchen exit. He had come to believe that if he let his guard down for even a moment, something would find him—a gas leak, a stray sound, a touch from behind that he had not anticipated. The startle response became a constant humiliation; a colleague once tapped his shoulder to ask a question, and Kwame spun around with a shout, his hands up in a defensive stance. After that, he tried to stand with his back to a wall whenever possible.

The cost of all this vigilance was a kind of quiet erosion. His marriage began to feel like a distant thing, built more on avoidance than on connection. Miriam stopped asking why he did not want to go to the movies or to family dinners; she just arranged her own plans. Kwame noticed that he could no longer tolerate being home alone on his day off—the silence was too loud, too likely to be broken by the wrong sound—so he went to work even when he was not scheduled. His boss commented that he was burning out, and for the first time, Kwame admitted to himself that he might be breaking down.

What brought him into the clinic, finally, was a simple moment: he was driving home from a double shift, and a truck backfired in the lane next to him. He jerked the wheel, nearly hitting a curb, and pulled over, shaking. He sat there for twenty minutes, unable to move, while the antiseptic smell of his own sweat reminded him of that hospital gurney. When he got home, Miriam was waiting with a phone number. She did not say much, just handed it to him. He took it, and now he sits in a therapist’s waiting room, terrified of what might come next but more afraid of what will happen if he keeps running. He hopes, without quite believing it, that somewhere past the scanning and the startle and the constant planning for escape, there might be a version of himself who can just walk into a room.
